# Alchemy

The art of transformation — part proto-chemistry, part philosophy, part
contemplative practice. This repository collects notes on its substances,
processes, practitioners, and primary texts.

## The tria prima

Paracelsus reduced the material world to three principles:

- [[mercury]] — the volatile spirit
- [[sulphur]] — the combustible soul
- [[salt]] — the fixed body

## Substances

- [prima materia](/substances/prima-materia.md) — the undifferentiated first matter
- [the philosophers' stone](/substances/philosophers-stone.md) — the goal of the Great Work

## Processes

The [magnum opus](/processes/magnum-opus.md) organizes the operations into
stages. Individual operations are documented separately:

- [calcination](/processes/calcination.md)
- [dissolution](/processes/dissolution.md)
- [coagulation](/processes/coagulation.md)

## Practitioners

| Practitioner | Tradition | Approximate era |
|---|---|---|
| [Maria Prophetissa](/practitioners/maria-prophetissa.md) | Alexandrian | 3rd century |
| [Jabir ibn Hayyan](/practitioners/jabir-ibn-hayyan.md) | Islamic | 8th century |
| [Paracelsus](/practitioners/paracelsus.md) | Western | 16th century |
| [Isaac Newton](/practitioners/newton.md) | Western | 17th century |

## Texts

- [The Emerald Tablet](/texts/emerald-tablet.md)
- [Mutus Liber](/texts/mutus-liber.md)

# Laboratory notes — January

Bench work on [calcination](/processes/calcination.md), chasing the weight gain.

operator:: bb
balance:: analytical

## Setup

Lead sheet cut into 2 g pieces, crucible pre-fired to constant weight, muffle at
600 °C. Weighings after cooling in a desiccator.

```text
tare crucible → weigh Pb → 600C 2h → cool in desiccator → reweigh
```

## Results

| Run | Pb in (g) | Calx out (g) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.001 | 2.140 | +0.139 |
| 2 | 2.004 | 2.147 | +0.143 |
| 3 | 1.998 | 2.138 | +0.140 |

Consistent gain of about 7% by mass. The colour went yellow then, on longer
heating, red — massicot to minium, as expected.

The gain is real and reproducible on a bench with 1830s-grade equipment. Anyone
doing this carefully before Lavoisier had the fact in hand; what was missing was
a framework that could accept it.

## Side work

Burned a batch of wormwood to ash and leached it while the muffle was up to
temperature: 40 g dried herb gave 1.1 g of crude salt after a single
recrystallization. That is the [[salt]] of the tria prima, obtained in an
afternoon, and it is easy to see why the operation carried evidential weight.

Sulphide colours are next — sulphur over the same metals, recording colour
against stoichiometry.

## Safety

Mercury work deferred — see [[mercury]] for the toxicity notes. Not handling it
without a fume hood.

## Tasks

- [x] Pre-fire crucibles to constant weight
- [x] Three replicate runs on lead
- [x] Record the colour sequence
- [x] Extract the salt of wormwood and weigh the yield
- [ ] Repeat the series with copper
- [ ] Plot mass gain against heating time
- [ ] Tabulate the metal sulphides by colour

# Laboratory notes — February

Recrystallization series on alum, testing the "purity gain per cycle" claim from
[coagulation](/processes/coagulation.md).

operator:: bb
balance:: analytical

## Method

Saturate at 80 °C, filter hot through a warmed funnel, cool undisturbed to room
temperature overnight, harvest, then re-saturate the mother liquor.

```text
saturate 80C → hot filter → cool overnight → harvest → repeat on liquor
```

## Results

| Cycle | Crop (g) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 14.2 | large clean octahedra |
| 2 | 5.8 | slightly smaller, still clear |
| 3 | 1.9 | small, some inclusions |
| 4 | 0.4 | poor, cloudy |

Yield falls off fast. Crystal quality is best in cycle 1 and degrades as
impurities concentrate in the liquor — the opposite of the alchemical expectation
that repeated cycling *improves* the product indefinitely.

The refinement is real but bounded, and it plateaus by cycle 3. That is exactly
the asymptote the tradition mistook for a trajectory.

## Conclusion

`solve et coagula` purifies. It does not transform. The claim in
[the philosophers' stone](/substances/philosophers-stone.md) does not follow from
this bench behaviour, and would not have followed for anyone who weighed the
crops.

## Tasks

- [x] Four recrystallization cycles with weights
- [x] Note crystal quality per cycle
- [ ] Assay cycle 1 and cycle 4 crops for iron
- [ ] Write the plateau result up for the coagulation note

# Jabir ibn Hayyan

8th–9th century, the towering figure of the Islamic alchemical tradition, and the
source — through the Latin *Geber* — of most of what medieval Europe knew.

known_for:: mercury-sulphur theory
century:: 8

## The mercury–sulphur theory

Every metal is a compound of [[mercury]] and [[sulphur]]; the proportion and the
purity of the mixture determine which metal you have. Gold is the balanced,
perfectly mixed case.

The consequence is the whole transmutation programme: if lead and gold differ
only in proportion, changing lead into gold requires no new substance, just
rebalancing. This is a *coherent* research question given the premises, and it
kept competent people busy for eight centuries.

## Method

More important than the theory is the insistence on procedure. The Jabirian
corpus specifies quantities, apparatus, and sequence, and expects the reader to
reproduce the result. It describes the preparation of what became the mineral
acids — see [dissolution](/processes/dissolution.md) — and classifies substances
by observable behaviour rather than by symbol.

That is recognisably experimental practice, several centuries before the
vocabulary existed for it.

## The corpus problem

Thousands of works bear the name; they cannot all be one author. The consensus is
a school writing under an authoritative name over generations. Attribution
questions remain open.

- [ ] Separate the Jabirian corpus into strata by vocabulary

# Maria Prophetissa

Alexandrian alchemist, probably 1st–3rd century, known only through quotation.
The earliest named practitioner whose *apparatus* survives in continuous use.

known_for:: balneum mariae
century:: 3

## The water bath

The *balneum Mariae* — Mary's bath — is a vessel heated indirectly by sitting it
in hot water. It holds a temperature that cannot exceed the boiling point of
water, which is exactly what you want for anything that scorches.

It is still standard equipment, still called a bain-marie, and it works for the
same reason it always did. Very little else in the alchemical inventory has that
record.

She is also credited with the *tribikos*, a three-armed still, and the *kerotakis*,
a sealed vessel for exposing metals to vapours.

## The axiom

> One becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the one as the
> fourth.

Quoted endlessly and explained never. Readings range from a distillation
schedule to a numerological gloss on the four stages of the
[magnum opus](/processes/magnum-opus.md). The honest position is that we do not
know what she meant.

## Assessment

Her reputation rests on hardware, not theory — and the hardware was right. Among
the practitioners here she is the one whose contribution needed no correction.

# Isaac Newton

1643–1727. Wrote more on alchemy than on physics, and published none of it.

known_for:: unpublished alchemical corpus
century:: 17

## Scale of the work

Roughly a million words of alchemical manuscript survive: transcriptions,
indexes of authors, and his own laboratory records with quantities and dates. He
kept furnaces at Trinity for decades and ran the work himself rather than
delegating it.

Keynes, who bought a large part of the papers at auction in 1936, called him
"the last of the magicians." The phrase is memorable and slightly unfair — the
notebooks are methodical, quantitative, and unmystical in tone.

## The index of authors

His *Index Chemicus* cross-references hundreds of alchemical texts by topic. It
is a serious piece of scholarship on a corpus he expected to contain a real
secret, encoded.

That expectation was the error, and it was not a careless one: the tradition
*claimed* to encode a secret, and Newton took the claim at face value and tested
it with the most rigorous method available. The method was sound; the corpus was
empty.

## Why it matters here

Newton is the clean case against reading alchemy as mere credulity. The most
capable investigator of the era worked the programme for thirty years with full
rigour and got nothing, because there was nothing there. That is a result, and
the [magnum opus](/processes/magnum-opus.md) framework does not survive it.

- [ ] Read the Index Chemicus entries on [[mercury]]
- [ ] Cross-check the furnace dates against the Principia years

# Paracelsus

Theophrastus von Hohenheim, 1493–1541. Redirected alchemy from metallurgy to
medicine, and was insufferable about it.

known_for:: tria prima
century:: 16

## The tria prima

He replaced the four elements with three principles — [[mercury]], [[sulphur]],
[[salt]] — as the constituents of every body. See [index](/index.md) for the
scheme.

As chemistry this is wrong. As a research programme it was an improvement: the
tria prima are *operationally defined* by what happens when you heat a substance
and see what flies off, what burns, and what remains. The four elements are not
defined by any operation at all.

## Iatrochemistry

His real contribution: minerals as medicines, prepared by chemical operation and
dosed by weight. Mercury for syphilis, antimony as an emetic, laudanum for pain.
Some of these worked. Several were poisons.

> All things are poison and nothing is without poison; only the dose makes a
> thing not a poison.

That is the founding statement of dose–response, and it is correct.

## Character

He burned Avicenna's books publicly, lectured in German rather than Latin,
insulted the faculty of every university that employed him, and was run out of
Basel. His posthumous reputation was built by followers who systematized what he
left as invective.

- [ ] Check which mineral remedies survived into the 18th-century pharmacopoeia
- [x] Confirm the dose–response quotation's source

# Calcination

Heating a substance in air until it is reduced to a friable powder — a *calx*.
The first of the twelve gates and, in practice, the first thing anyone does.

element:: fire
reversible:: no

## Procedure

Grind the material, spread it thinly in an open crucible, and heat steadily
below the melting point. Stir to expose fresh surface. Continue until no further
weight is lost and no fumes come off.

```text
crucible → grind → thin layer → moderate heat → stir → constant weight
```

The endpoint is the constant weight, not the colour. Colour tells you which
oxide you have; weight tells you that you are finished.

## What is actually happening

Organic matter burns away; metals take up oxygen. The characteristic *gain* in
weight when calcining a metal is the observation that eventually broke the
phlogiston theory — the calx weighs more than the metal, which a theory of
escaping substance cannot accommodate.

Alchemical practice recorded this gain for centuries without drawing the
inference. The data were sound; the framework could not use them.

## Products

- calcined lead → yellow massicot, then red minium
- calcined copper → black tenorite
- plant matter → ash, source of the [[salt]]

## Tasks

- [x] Verify the weight gain on lead with a balance
- [ ] Repeat with copper and record the colour sequence

# Coagulation

The *coagula* half of *solve et coagula*: bringing a dissolved substance back to
a solid, ideally more ordered than before. Crystallization, precipitation, and
slow evaporation all count.

element:: earth
reversible:: yes

## Why it closes the work

Dissolution destroys structure; coagulation rebuilds it. The pair is the engine
of the whole programme — the claim being that matter repeatedly dissolved and
recoagulated is progressively refined, and that enough cycles yield the
[philosophers' stone](/substances/philosophers-stone.md).

The claim is false, but the intuition is not absurd: recrystallization *does*
purify, and each cycle *does* leave a cleaner product. The error is extrapolating
an asymptote into a transformation.

## Practical notes

Slow is better. Rapid cooling gives small, impure crystals that trap solvent;
slow evaporation at a stable temperature gives large clean ones.

```text
saturate hot → filter while hot → cool undisturbed → harvest → repeat on liquor
```

Repeating on the mother liquor is where the yield is. See the
[February notes](/lab/2026-02-notes.md) for a worked run.

## Tasks

- [x] Recrystallize alum three times and weigh each crop
- [ ] Measure purity gain per cycle to find where it plateaus

# Dissolution

Taking the calx into a liquid — *solve* of the maxim *solve et coagula*. The
second gate, and the operation that produced most of alchemy's real chemical
discoveries.

element:: water
reversible:: yes

## Solvents

The search for solvents is where the practical payoff was. Distilling vitriol
and nitre gave the mineral acids, and those genuinely dissolve things nothing
else will:

```text
nitre + vitriol      → aqua fortis     (nitric acid)
aqua fortis + sal    → aqua regia      (dissolves gold)
```

*Aqua regia* — royal water, because it dissolves the royal metal — is the single
most consequential thing to come out of the laboratory tradition. It is a real
reagent, it does something no other liquid does, and its discovery was driven
entirely by the transmutation programme.

## The alkahest

The hypothetical universal solvent, said to dissolve any substance into its
prima materia. Never produced. The obvious objection — that no vessel could hold
it — was raised at the time and answered with the claim that it dissolves only
what is imperfect.

This is unfalsifiable, and its defenders were not troubled by that.

# The magnum opus

The Great Work: the full sequence that carries the matter from its raw state to
the [philosophers' stone](/substances/philosophers-stone.md). The operations vary
between authors; the *colour sequence* is remarkably stable.

## The four stages

| Stage | Colour | Sense |
|---|---|---|
| Nigredo | black | putrefaction, reduction to [prima materia](/substances/prima-materia.md) |
| Albedo | white | washing, purification |
| Citrinitas | yellow | dawning of the solar principle |
| Rubedo | red | the completed stone |

Later writers frequently drop citrinitas, giving a three-colour scheme. The
compression is worth noting: it tracks a shift from observing the vessel to
allegorizing the soul.

## Why colour

Colour change is the one signal a pre-instrumental laboratory can read reliably.
It is reproducible, it is public, and it does not depend on the operator's
judgement. Building the whole framework on the colour sequence was, given the
available instruments, a reasonable methodological choice.

## Operations

The twelve gates assign operations to the stages. The three documented here:

- [calcination](/processes/calcination.md) — nigredo
- [dissolution](/processes/dissolution.md) — nigredo into albedo
- [coagulation](/processes/coagulation.md) — rubedo

## Open questions

- [ ] Map the twelve gates onto the four stages across three sources
- [ ] Decide whether citrinitas is dropped or absorbed

# Mercury

Quicksilver: a metal that is liquid at room temperature, and therefore the
obvious emblem of everything that refuses to hold a fixed form.

symbol:: ☿
melting_point:: -38.8
toxic:: yes

## As a principle

In the tria prima, mercury is the volatile spirit — the part of a substance that
can be driven off and recondensed. It stands opposite [[salt]], the fixed body,
with [[sulphur]] mediating.

| Principle | Role | Fixed? |
|---|---|---|
| Mercury | spirit | no |
| Sulphur | soul | partly |
| Salt | body | yes |

## As a material

Mercury dissolves gold and silver into amalgams, which made it indispensable to
assayers and irresistible to alchemists: a substance that visibly *takes gold
into itself* invites the inference that it can also give gold back.

It is also poisonous, a fact the laboratory notes record without connecting it
to the tremors and mania that follow long exposure. See the
[January notes](/lab/2026-01-notes.md) for handling precautions.

## Reading

- [Paracelsus](/practitioners/paracelsus.md) on the tria prima
- [Jabir ibn Hayyan](/practitioners/jabir-ibn-hayyan.md) on the mercury–sulphur theory of metals

# The philosophers' stone

The *lapis philosophorum* is the end of the [magnum opus](/processes/magnum-opus.md):
a substance said to transmute base metals into gold and to perfect whatever it
touches.

appearance:: red
also_known_as:: lapis
transmutes:: lead

## Claims

Three powers are attributed to it, in descending order of plausibility:

1. **Transmutation** of lead or mercury into gold.
2. **Medicine** — the *panacea*, curing illness and extending life.
3. **Perfection** of the practitioner, the stone being a mirror of the soul.

The third reading dominates the later literature, where the laboratory work is
explicitly allegorical.

## Preparation

Every account is incomplete, and deliberately so. The common skeleton:

- reduce the matter to [prima materia](/substances/prima-materia.md)
- carry it through the four stages of the [[magnum-opus]]
- fix the volatile and volatilize the fixed

Compare [[mercury]], whose duality the stone is supposed to resolve.

## Open questions

- The surviving transmutation claims have never been gathered in one place with
  dates and provenance attached.
- The shift from literal to allegorical readings is well documented; what caused
  it is still disputed.

# Prima materia

The *prima materia* is the formless first matter from which all substances are
composed — not a reagent you can order, but the state a substance is reduced to
before it can be rebuilt.

state:: undifferentiated
obtainable:: no

## Descriptions

The texts are deliberately evasive. It is called the dragon, the chaos, the
lead of the philosophers, the vile black earth. Practitioners took this
multiplicity as proof that the *prima materia* is a condition rather than an
ingredient.

> That which is below is like that which is above.

The [Emerald Tablet](/texts/emerald-tablet.md) is usually read as describing
this reduction and return.

## Relation to the Great Work

Reduction to the *prima materia* is the purpose of [[nigredo]], the blackening
that opens the [magnum opus](/processes/magnum-opus.md). [Calcination](/processes/calcination.md)
is the usual first operation.

## Open questions

- Whether the "chaos" and the "lead of the philosophers" readings can be
  reconciled, or whether they simply belong to different schools.
- How far the term can honestly be traced back through the Alexandrian corpus
  before it becomes a later retrojection.

# Salt

What remains. Burn a plant to ash and leach the ash with water, and the residue
that crystallizes out is the salt — the incombustible, fixed body.

symbol:: 🜔
soluble:: yes
toxic:: no

## As a principle

Salt is the third of the tria prima: the body that gives a substance its
persistence and form. Where [[mercury]] flies off and [[sulphur]] burns, salt
stays behind.

The operation that produces it is straightforward and repeatable, which gave the
principle an evidential weight the other two lacked. You can *show* someone the
salt of a plant.

## Practical extraction

The standard route, still sound:

1. Incinerate the material completely — see [calcination](/processes/calcination.md).
2. Leach the ash with distilled water.
3. Filter, then evaporate slowly to crystallize.

[Coagulation](/processes/coagulation.md) is the general name for step 3.

## Note

The alchemical "salt" is not sodium chloride but the mixed carbonates and
potash left after combustion. The terminology predates the distinction.

## Supplies

Bench stock for the leaching work. Nothing outstanding.

- [x] Buy more salt of tartar
- [x] Replace the leaching filter papers

# Sulphur

Brimstone: yellow, brittle, and burns with a blue flame and a choking smell.
Its behaviour under heat made it the natural emblem of combustibility.

symbol:: 🜍
melting_point:: 115.2
toxic:: mildly

## As a principle

Sulphur is the soul — the combustible principle, what makes a substance
flammable and gives it colour and character. It mediates between the volatile
[[mercury]] and the fixed [[salt]].

In the mercury–sulphur theory inherited from
[Jabir ibn Hayyan](/practitioners/jabir-ibn-hayyan.md), every metal is a
compound of the two, and the proportions determine the metal. Gold is a perfect
balance; lead is the same pair badly mixed. Transmutation therefore requires no
new matter, only a correction of proportion — which is why the theory was so
durable and so encouraging.

## As a material

Sulphur combines directly with most metals on heating, producing sulphides whose
colours are dramatic and reproducible. This is genuinely useful chemistry, and
much of the practical content of the alchemical corpus concerns it. The bench
work is tracked in the [January notes](/lab/2026-01-notes.md).

# The Emerald Tablet

*Tabula Smaragdina.* A few hundred words attributed to Hermes Trismegistus,
earliest surviving in Arabic around the 8th century, and the most quoted text in
the entire tradition.

length:: short
attributed_to:: hermes

## The text

> That which is above is from that which is below, and that which is below is
> from that which is above, working the miracles of one.

> And as all things have been and arose from one by the mediation of one, so all
> things have their birth from this one thing by adaptation.

## Why it dominated

It is short enough to memorize, concrete enough to sound like instructions, and
vague enough to support any reading. Every practitioner from
[Jabir](/practitioners/jabir-ibn-hayyan.md) to [Newton](/practitioners/newton.md)
produced a commentary, and the commentaries agree on nothing.

Newton's translation survives in his own hand. He read it, plausibly, as
describing distillation and condensation — the below rising and the above
returning — which maps onto [dissolution](/processes/dissolution.md) and
[coagulation](/processes/coagulation.md).

## Assessment

Read as chemistry it says nothing operational. Read as a statement that the same
laws hold at every scale, it is a decent piece of natural philosophy that happens
to be true, arrived at for no good reason.

# Mutus Liber

The "silent book," La Rochelle, 1677: fifteen engraved plates and essentially no
text. The entire Great Work, allegedly, in pictures.

length:: fifteen plates
attributed_to:: altus

## Contents

The plates show a couple gathering dew in sheets stretched between poles,
processing it through vessels, and attending a furnace, framed by angels and
zodiacal signs. A sequence is clearly intended. What it instructs is not clear.

The dew-gathering is the one concretely readable operation, and it connects to a
real strand of practice: dew was held to be a celestial condensate and a candidate
[prima materia](/substances/prima-materia.md).

## Status of these notes

Draft. I have not worked through the plates in order against a commentary, and
the secondary literature disagrees about even the number of stages depicted.

# Calcination

Heating a substance in air until it is reduced to a friable powder — a *calx*.
The first of the twelve gates and, in practice, the first thing anyone does.

element:: fire
reversible:: no

## Procedure

Grind the material, spread it thinly in an open crucible, and heat steadily
below the melting point. Stir to expose fresh surface. Continue until no further
weight is lost and no fumes come off.

```text
crucible → grind → thin layer → moderate heat → stir → constant weight
```

The endpoint is the constant weight, not the colour. Colour tells you which
oxide you have; weight tells you that you are finished.

## What is actually happening

Organic matter burns away; metals take up oxygen. The characteristic *gain* in
weight when calcining a metal is the observation that eventually broke the
phlogiston theory — the calx weighs more than the metal, which a theory of
escaping substance cannot accommodate.

Alchemical practice recorded this gain for centuries without drawing the
inference. The data were sound; the framework could not use them.

## Products

- calcined lead → yellow massicot, then red minium
- calcined copper → black tenorite
- plant matter → ash, source of the [[salt]]

## Tasks

- [x] Verify the weight gain on lead with a balance
- [ ] Repeat with copper and record the colour sequence
- [ ] Chase down the earliest recorded weight-gain measurement

# Salt

What remains. Burn a plant to ash and leach the ash with water, and the residue
that crystallizes out is the salt — the incombustible, fixed body.

symbol:: 🜔
soluble:: yes
toxic:: no

## As a principle

Salt is the third of the tria prima: the body that gives a substance its
persistence and form. Where [[mercury]] flies off and [[sulphur]] burns, salt
stays behind.

The operation that produces it is straightforward and repeatable, which gave the
principle an evidential weight the other two lacked. You can *show* someone the
salt of a plant.

## Practical extraction

The standard route, still sound:

1. Incinerate the material completely — see [calcination](/processes/calcination.md).
2. Leach the ash with distilled water.
3. Filter, then evaporate slowly to crystallize.

[Coagulation](/processes/coagulation.md) is the general name for step 3.

## Note

The alchemical "salt" is not sodium chloride but the mixed carbonates and
potash left after combustion. The terminology predates the distinction.

## Supplies

Bench stock for the leaching work. Nothing outstanding.

- [x] Buy more salt of tartar
- [x] Replace the leaching filter papers

# query — OQX syntax reference

The `query` tool takes ONE plain OQX string (+ optional `limit`/`cursor`, and
`bare: true` to drop the automatic `id`/`path` envelope — needs a `select`).
There is no {from, filter, order} envelope: every concern is a clause of the
string. Two rules tell the two syntaxes apart: DOT navigation belongs to the
host object model (`doc.layer`, `section.blocks`, `dst.title`); WHITESPACE
query directives belong to OQX — a nested query is `<receiver> collect|exists|
count|first|single { <block> }` (a postfix directive + a `{ … }` block), never a
method. Its distinctive power is the receiver-constrained nested query that
correlates to the current row: `from docs where nodes exists { where kind ==
"md:task" }` returns only the docs that themselves contain a matching node.

  [select <items>] from <target> [where <pred>] [frontier <pred>] [follow <dest> [{ … }], …]
                   [group by <key>, …] [having <pred>] [order by <expr> [asc|desc], …] [limit N] [offset N]
  <target> count|exists|none|first|single { <block> }     (scalar/one-row form: a bare target at the root scope)

CLAUSE ORDER IS FIXED: select, from, where, frontier, follow, group by, having, order by, limit, offset —
each at most once; an out-of-order clause is a parse error naming the order.
Only `select` may drop its keyword, and only as the first clause
(`path, era from docs where …`). A top-level predicate needs `where`, because
`where` follows `from` (`era > 1600 from docs` is the clause-order error); a
block may LEAD with a predicate (see Sugar), but a predicate after a projection
still needs the keyword (`{ name where kind == "md:task" }`, not
`{ name, kind == "md:task" }`); `from docs count` is an error (write
`docs count { … }`). `where` and later `select` items may use the same body's
`select` aliases (`select path, old: era < 1000 from docs where old`; an alias
shadows a same-named field there). `and` / `or` / `not` are the connectives;
the symbols `&&` / `||` / `!` are accepted synonyms (the words are canonical and
what `print` writes).

## Sugar (OQX 0.17)

Every form here is shorthand for an explicit directive (the AST is the explicit form):
  nodes { kind == "md:task" }        ≡ nodes collect { where kind == "md:task" } — a receiver block with
                                       no consumer is collect; a block whose LEADING expression is a predicate
                                       (comparison, call, !/is/not, in, literal, (…), a consumer test — anything
                                       but a bare name, a dotted path or a ^lift) is where-first. Bare names still
                                       project: nodes { name } ≡ nodes collect { name }; filter a bare field with
                                       nodes { is checked }. Wherever a value stands (0.20), call arguments included:
                                       size(children { is checked }); x distinct { … } ≡ x collect distinct { … }. After a
                                       follow destination too: follow children { depth 2 } is that destination's block.
  (a, b)                              a tuple (0.20): two or more expressions, concatenated one level flat — a value
                                       (size((tags, aliases)), "x" in (tags, aliases)) and a receiver ((a, b) { … },
                                       follow (before, after) { depth 2 }); (a) alone is grouping
  refs(x)[0]                          ≡ refs(x) first { offset 0 }   positional (integer literal or ${binding});
                                       out of range ⇒ absent; refs(x)[0].path navigates the row
  ^docs[path == ^company]             ≡ ^docs first { where path == ^company }   first match or absent
  ^docs[path == ^company]!            ≡ … single { … } required: exactly one, else filter_invalid
  title!                              required: title, or an error naming the expression (and the row's $key — its id)
                                       — never a filter, never a coercion (0!, ""! are values); tightest: a!.b vs a.b!
  is x / not x                        truthiness of x, and its negation (prefix; `not` ≡ `!`)
  x is y / x is not y                 identity ($key: a store row's id, else structural) — compares rows, which == does not;
                                       x is null = absent; for scalars is ≡ ==; comparison precedence, no chaining
  a and b / a or b                    the connectives (≡ && / ||: same precedence, short-circuit, value: data.title or path coalesces)
  boss: ^docs[path == ^manager], bossName: boss.title   a select item may use the items to its LEFT
  Reserved words (never a bare field name): from where select is not and or, true false null.
  Contextual words (limit order offset follow collect count first distinct desc by in frontier depth) parse as
  fields in expression position (select o: order from docs).

Results are LEAN hits — { id, path } + whatever `select` projects (or `values`,
`count`, `exists`, `none`). The envelope keys ARE the attributes: copy a hit's
`id` straight into `where id == "…"` (no translation); `select id, path` is simply
the envelope (no duplicate columns); any OTHER projection whose output key would
be `id` or `path` must be aliased — `select data.path` is refused ("projection
`path` collides with the hit envelope — alias it (`p: data.path`)"); a row
surfacing as a value (an empty `collect { }`) is the same `{ id, path }`. Every
other tool spells a row the same way (`docs_read` → `{ id, path, rev, properties,
raw }`, `blocks_read` → `{ id, type, text, raw, hash, … }`, `docs_list` → `{ id,
path, updated_at, blocks }`, a revision → `{ id, path, hash }`): hydrate by id via
blocks_read/docs_read.

## Paths

Every path the surface returns is `/`-rooted — the form a reference is
written in (`[x](/projects/oqx.md)`, `before: [/timeline/kickoff.md]`): a
hit's `path`, an edge's `dst_path`, every tool's paths. Every path it
accepts tolerates both forms (`/a.md` or `a.md`): tool arguments, `refs(x)`,
`within(...)`, and a string LITERAL compared with `path`/`dst_path` (bare, or
through a row handle: `doc.path`) by `==`/`!=` or passed to their
`.startsWith(...)` (it is rooted first, so `path == "a.md"` and `path == "/a.md"`
both match). A property holding a reference compares directly — and is never
rooted: `where ^path in list(after)`, `where customer == ^path`,
`where data.path == "/x.md"` (the author's `path:` key, as written) — no
`"/" + ...` glue.

## Targets & field namespaces

THE NAME RULE: `$` belongs to OQX — $it, $key, $depth, $stop, $leaf, $frontier,
$ordinal are values the LANGUAGE injects into a scope; omgbase adds NO $ names
(a `$id` in a query is an unknown name, absent). Every engine attribute is a BARE
snake_case name that WINS on collision — the convention the relations (children,
blocks, out, in, doc, frontmatter, …) always followed: a bare name that is an
engine attribute reads the engine's value, never yours. Your data is bare too;
where a key of yours collides with an engine name, reach it through a source
handle: `data.<k>` (the merged authored view — frontmatter + inline, exactly the
read a bare non-colliding key performs), `frontmatter.<k>`, `inline.<k>`. So
`path` is the engine's /-rooted location and `data.path` your `path:` key;
`tags` is your tags ∪ the body #hashtags and `data.tags` the authored list alone;
`title` the computed title (the first H1) and `data.title` your `title:`;
`entries(data)` lists every authored top-level key. Same value, same name
everywhere: a hit's `id` is docs_read's `id` and the `id` argument of blocks_read.

  Reserved bare names per kind (engine attributes; handles; self; relations):
    docs    id path raw hash updated_at title tags format | data frontmatter inline | doc | blocks nodes out_links in_links revisions
    blocks  id path doc_id raw hash updated_at type text attrs depth ordinal | block doc | children nodes out_links section
    nodes   id path doc_id block_id kind name value attrs | section doc block | blocks subsections children
    links   id path doc_id block_id via_id dst_id dst_path uri field dst_kind predicate provenance anchor | doc
    revisions  id path rev seq doc_id commit ts origin actor reason hash is_current | doc
  A key of yours with any of these names is `data.<k>` (or frontmatter.<k> /
  inline.<k> by source; attrs.<k> on a block or node).
  UNKNOWN NAMES: a name that is none of the above AND that no object of the
  kind in this repository carries is reported before any row is read — on
  links as a filter_invalid error naming the fields; on docs/blocks/nodes the
  result gains `hints` (one line per name, nearest match when there is one)
  and the rows still come back; in a plan/apply/execute selector it is refused.
  A property some objects carry is known (partial presence is normal).

docs:
  - bare identifier  = a document PROPERTY (frontmatter + inline `key:: value`,
                       unioned; nested via dots: meta.owner). YAML/JSON docs
                       expose the parsed object's keys the same way.
  - source handles   = data.<k> (merged authored view) / frontmatter.<k> /
                       inline.<k>; the whole bag as a collection via entries(data)
                       / entries(frontmatter) / entries(inline) (see entries()).
  - attributes       = id, path (/-rooted, see Paths), updated_at (ISO-8601,
                       sorts chronologically), raw (the whole file, frontmatter
                       included), hash (its sha256, 64 hex), title (the computed
                       title: the first H1; data.title is the authored key), tags
                       (authored tags ∪ body #hashtags, deduped, authored first;
                       data.tags is the authored list), format (the doc's format —
                       "markdown"/"yaml"/"json"; present on EVERY doc, so
                       has(format) is always true and `format == "yaml"` is the
                       filter).
  - relations        = nodes, blocks, doc.out_links / doc.in_links (a doc's
                       links as rows; the documents at their other end are
                       out_links collect distinct { from dst } and
                       in_links collect distinct { from doc } — there is no
                       out / in relation), revisions (the document's stored
                       revisions, oldest first — see revisions below).

blocks:
  - bare fields      = doc_id (the owning doc), type, text (normalized), ordinal
                       (0-based among siblings), depth (0 at the top level), and
                       every attrs key FLATTENED onto the row (bare `checked`
                       reads attrs.checked; `attrs.<k>` still works; the
                       structural fields win on collision; absent ⇒ false).
  - attributes       = id, path (the owning doc's path), raw (the block's raw
                       source — a container's raw holds its children), hash
                       (its sha256 — the value update/split expect as
                       expect.content_hash), updated_at.
  - reach-through    = doc.<key> / doc.path / doc.id / doc.format = the
                       CONTAINING doc (doc.id and doc.path cost nothing — they
                       read the row's own doc_id / joined path, no lookup).
  - relations        = block.children, block.nodes, block.out_links, section.
  NOTE: inside a `follow`, $depth/$ordinal are ALWAYS the walk's metadata; a
  block's own nesting is `depth` / `ordinal` (no $) everywhere.

nodes:
  - bare fields      = doc_id, block_id (null for a block-less node), kind
                       (md:task / md:link / md:section / yaml:…), name, value,
                       + attrs keys flattened (checked, level).
  - attributes       = id, path.
  - reach-through    = doc.<key> / doc.id / doc.path, block.type / block.text
                       / block.id / block.path.
  - relations        = section.blocks, section.children, section.subsections.

links:  (the authored link graph as rows — one per open link: the relation a link
        establishes; the md:link NODE is its occurrence in the text and via_id
        points at it — a frontmatter link has a row and no node)
  - bare fields      = doc_id (the SOURCE doc), block_id (the source block; null
                       for a frontmatter edge), via_id, dst_id (the destination
                       node id: a doc id, an external node id or phantom:<path>),
                       dst_path (target doc path, /-rooted; NULL when
                       dangling/external), uri (external URL; NULL otherwise),
                       predicate ("references"/"embeds"/freeform), provenance
                       ("link"/"frontmatter"/"inline_field"/…), dst_kind
                       ("document"/"external"/"collection"), anchor, field (the
                       frontmatter key / inline field it was authored in).
  - attributes       = id, path (the SOURCE doc's path); doc.<key> reaches the
                       source document. There is no from_commit: a query sees
                       open edges only (history is blocks_history/changes_since).
  - text()/semantic() are N/A on links.

revisions:  (history as rows — one per stored revision of every document of the
        repository, deleted documents included: what docs_history lists, queryable)
  - bare fields      = rev (= id), seq (1, 2, … per document), doc_id, commit,
                       ts (the commit's time, sorts chronologically), origin
                       ("observed"/"api"/"import"/"projection"), actor, reason,
                       hash (the rendered file's sha256 — docs_history's hash),
                       is_current (true for the document's current revision).
  - attributes       = id (the revision id, r_…), path (the path the revision
                       was committed under — a move re-paths only the current
                       revision, so earlier ones keep the old path). doc.<key>
                       reaches the document's CURRENT row; absent for a deleted
                       document, so where doc == null is the revisions of deleted documents.
  - on docs          = revisions is a relation (oldest first): a document with
                       more than one version is docs { revisions count { } > 1 }.
  - text()/semantic() are N/A on revisions. The body as of a revision is
    docs_read { path, at: "<rev>" } (docs_read_at is the same call).

## Scoping (ADR-015; the root row since surface 2.0): bare names are LOCAL

  name          the CURRENT row only — never falls through to an enclosing row
                or the repository; an absent field is simply absent.
  ^name         one scope OUT (the enclosing row's fields/intrinsics/lifts);
                ^^name two scopes out. `^path` = the enclosing row's path.
  ^docs ^nodes ^blocks ^links ^revisions
                THE ROOT ROW (surface 2.0, oqx 0.18): the repository is the root
                scope's row, one scope out from a top-level row, so ^docs there is
                the whole documents scan (uncorrelated until you add a ^ predicate);
                one caret per enclosing block (^^docs from depth two), or the
                absolute 0^docs from ANY depth. ^id / 0^id = the repository id.
                ^$it = the root object: ^$it.docs ≡ ^docs, entries(^$it) names the
                five collections. At the root scope itself a bare target is the scan
                (docs count { … }, from docs, entries(docs)).
                ERRORS: a bare `docs` INSIDE a block reads a property of the current
                row, which has none — refused ("did you mean ^docs"); `^docs` AT THE
                TOP LEVEL reaches past the root — refused (write the bare `docs`);
                so is `$repo` (surface < 2.0; the message names the replacement).
                nodes/blocks on a doc row are that doc's RELATIONS, not the root.
  $it           the current item itself (a row, or each ELEMENT when the
                receiver is a list property); ^$it = the enclosing row.
                $value is NOT an intrinsic (since oqx 0.15): it reads a
                property literally named $value, absent when there is none.
  $key          the row's identity (0.20): a store row's id (doc/block/node/edge), an entries(x)
                entry's key, a follow occurrence's walk identity; project $key: <expr> to rekey the
                rows a block yields (a destination block's $key: is not a column).

## Scalar semantics (@omgbase/oqx)

  comparisons  ==  !=  <  <=  >  >=    strict & typed (5 == "5" is false); either
                                       side may be a field (field-vs-field OK).
  absence      null and a missing field are the same "absent" value; two absents
               are EQUAL, so `absent != "x"` is TRUE and `absent == null` is TRUE.
               Relational (< <= > >=) on an absent operand → FALSE. Bare `f` in
               boolean position uses JS truthiness (absent/false/0/"" ⇒ false;
               NOTE: "false", [] and {} are truthy). has(f) = explicit presence.
  boolean      and  or  not    grouping ( … )   — && || ! are accepted synonyms
  arithmetic   + - * / %    (+ concatenates if either side is a string)
  membership   x in y       array → typed membership; string → substring;
                            object → key exists; range → coverage. Any list
                            property works directly: "pricing" in tags. list(f)
                            coerces scalar-or-list (absent → []) — use it when a
                            key is sometimes scalar, sometimes a list.
  ranges       lo..hi (inclusive)  lo...hi (exclusive hi)  ..hi  lo..
               era in 800..1680; works over ISO dates. range(prop) reads a
               range-shaped STRING property as an interval: "2026-01-15" in range(window).
  strings      x.contains("s") x.startsWith("p") x.endsWith("s") x.matches("^re$")
               (real regex) x.lower() x.upper() size(x). ALL CASE-SENSITIVE —
               fold with .lower(): title.lower().contains("aurora").
               Infix regex: x ~ "re" is x.matches("re"); x ~* "re" is the
               case-insensitive match; x !~ "re" and x !~* "re" negate them.
               Unanchored unless the pattern anchors; an absent x is false
               under ~ and TRUE under !~ (not SQL's NULL).
  functions    has(f)  size(x)  list(x)  entries(x)  range(s)
  dates        a date is an ISO string, a duration a NUMBER OF SECONDS; arithmetic
               is METHODS, never + or - (+ concatenates strings).
               date("today"|"now"|"yesterday"|"tomorrow"|"sow"|"eow"|"som"|"eom"|
               "soy"|"eoy") — the host clock, UTC; date("2026-10-15") canonical ISO
               (absent if unparseable). dur("1h30m") dur("2 days, 3 hours")
               dur("P1DT2H") dur(90) → seconds (year = 365 d, month = 30 d).
               d.plus(dur("30 days"))  d.minus(86400)  d.plus("1 month") (calendar:
               Jan 31 → Feb 28)  a.until(b) → signed seconds  d.year() d.month()
               d.day() d.weekday() (1 = Mon) d.hour() d.minute() d.second()
               d.date()  d.format("EEE dd MMM yyyy")  n.dur_text() → "1h 30m"
               n.dur_iso() → "PT1H30M". Total: a non-date is absent, so
               `where date(due) < date("today").minus(dur("30 days"))` just
               filters. A datetime is never < its own date: compare
               updated_at.date() == date("today"), or < date("tomorrow").
  literals     "str" 'str' 123 1.5 true false null
  determinism  no random; the only clock is date("today"/"now"/…), read once per
               query. Lists/structs are not literals; ternary is not supported.
               Errors surface as filter_invalid.
  scalars vs lists  a list-authored key never == a scalar (tags == "x" is false
               when tags is a list) — use `"x" in tags` / `in list(tags)`.

## Domain predicates (omgbase)

  text("terms")        FTS5 PRUNING predicate (docs match via their blocks, nodes
                       via the node index); composes anywhere, incl. nested scopes.
  semantic("phrase")   embedding cosine SCORE (docs/blocks): threshold it
                       (semantic("x") > 0.6), project it, or `order by semantic("x")
                       desc` for top-K. Needs a provider that has embedded the repository; else provider_unavailable.
  blocks target only:
    under(id_or_heading)      block in the containment subtree / section range
    under_heading("Launch")   an ancestor section heading contains the text (ci)
    under_kind(type[, name])  an ancestor block has that type (name: its text
                              contains / its key equals name)
    within("path" | "d_..")   containing doc = id, exact path, or path glob (*);
                              either path form
    yaml_path("a.b")          YAML docs: the block at that key path
    json_pointer("#/a/b")     JSON docs: the block at that pointer
    has_edge("pred"[, target])  an open authored edge with that predicate leaves here
    has_anchor()              block carries an authored ^ref
    parent_type() == "x"      parent block's type (must be compared)
    child_count() > 0         number of direct children (must be compared)
  refs(x)              the live documents a property's document references name:
                       x is a string, a list or absent; each "/a/b.md", "a/b.md"
                       or "d_…" element resolves to that doc's row; dangling and
                       non-string elements are dropped. Yields docs rows, so it is
                       a source, a receiver or a follow destination:
                       follow refs(before), refs(after) walks a timeline both ways.
                       The reverse direction needs no function: a document's
                       path is already the reference form, so
                       ^docs { where ^path in list(after) } is
                       "the documents whose `after` names me".
  A HIT IS A STORE ROW: a top-level row that is not a doc/block/node/edge fails
                       (filter_invalid). `follow before` over a list of paths
                       reaches the STRINGS — write `follow refs(before)`.

## Nested queries & consumers

  <receiver> collect|exists|none|count|first|single { <block> }
    receiver = a relation (nodes, blocks, doc.out_links, section.blocks, …), a
               reach-through row (dst, doc: one row — dst { title }), a
    list property (tags), entries(x), or a root collection (^docs; 0^docs at depth ≥ 2).
    block    = [select …] [from E] [where …] [frontier …] [follow …] [order by …] [limit N] [offset N]
               — the same fixed order as the top level (`from` optional; the
               receiver supplies the rows). A leading name/alias list is the
               projection (`select` dropped); a predicate always needs `where`.
               A `from E` inside a block RE-PROJECTS the rows through a relation
               (a typed flatMap): `docs collect { from nodes where kind == "md:task" }`
               starts at docs, projects each through `nodes`, and queries the
               resulting nodes; a scalar relation (`from doc`) contributes one
               row; a missing or non-navigable relation is a loud error, never a
               global scan.
  exists    ≥1 row      nodes exists { where kind == "md:task" and not checked }
  none      0 rows      nodes none { where kind == "md:task" and not checked }  ("every task done")
  count     a number    nodes count { where kind == "md:task" } >= 2
  collect   rows (default) — in select for nested results; in where with a lift
  first / single   zero-or-one (single errors on >1) — lookups in select
  distinct  on any consumer: dedup by projected value — nodes count distinct { select kind }
  limit/offset  bound the block's rows AFTER where/order/distinct, BEFORE the
            consumer reduces: nodes exists { offset 1 } = at least two;
            first { … offset 1 } = the second.
  lift      `^name:` in a where-collect binds values outward:
            select path, open from docs where nodes collect { ^open: value where kind == "md:task" and not checked }
  joins     ^<t> exists { where slug == ^ref }  semi-join; not … exists  anti-join;
            ^nodes single { where kind == "person" and attrs.id == ^owner_id }  lookup;
            x in ^keys  membership over a lifted set.

## select — projection

  select a, alias: expr, nested: nodes collect { … }
  bare key → the attribute when it is one (id, path, title, …), else the property
  (scalar-authored → scalar; list → array); data.<k> forces the property;
  a call/arithmetic needs an alias (n: size(tags)) unless in values mode;
  an output key of id/path other than the attribute itself needs an alias.
  raw         whole file bytes (docs) — docs_read is cheaper for one doc.
  distinct    select distinct type   (dedup hits by projected value)
  values      select <ONE item> values → bare values instead of records:
                select distinct type values from docs          → values: ["hub","lab-note",…]
                select path values from docs                   → values: ["/index.md", …]
                tags: tags collect { $it values }             → a plain array
                h: nodes first { name values where kind == "md:section" order by first_ordinal }
  entries(x)  a record as a collection ($key / $it per entry), key order:
                select fm: entries(data) collect { k: $key, v: $it }
                where entries(frontmatter) exists { where $key == "era" and $it > 1600 }
                entries(inline), entries(attrs), a nested map, or a list (index keys)
  $semantic_score is not a field — project semantic("…") under an alias instead.

## order by, limit/offset, pagination

  order by era desc, path asc      absent values sort LAST (asc); ties → (path, id)
  limit N / offset N               define the result SET (integer literals);
                                   the tool's limit/cursor then page WITHIN it
  cursor                           opaque keyset on (path,id); a custom order by
                                   disables it (you get the top page + truncated)

## Graph traversal (follow) and links

  The citation graph is the LINK ROWS walked through a destination block:
  dst is a link's destination document (absent for an external or dangling
  link — it then contributes no successor), doc its source.
  from docs where <seed> follow out_links collect { from dst }     docs the seed links TO
  from docs where <seed> follow in_links collect { from doc }      backlinks
    follow out_links collect { from dst depth 3 }                  bound (1..8, default 8) — a clause of the block
    follow out_links collect { from dst where layer == "canon" }   keep only matching successors
    follow in_links collect { from doc where ^path in list(before) }   ^ = the row being expanded
                                                   (^^ = the walk's enclosing scope)
    follow out_links collect { from dst where predicate == "depends_on" }   one predicate only
    follow out_links collect { from dst }, in_links collect { from doc }
                                                   several destinations: their union
                                                   (one step dedups by identity)
    follow ^docs { where out_links exists { where dst_path == ^^path } }
                                                   a destination block over the root's
                                                   documents, re-read per frontier row
                                                   (^ = that row) = the backlinks walk
    follow out_links collect { from dst frontier type == "practitioner" }   cut, keeping the frontier row
    from docs where type == "process" frontier !verified follow out_links collect { from dst }
                                                   the BODY's frontier applies to the seeds:
                                                   an unverified seed is kept, not expanded
    follow distinct out_links collect { from dst } / … { $key: group from dst }   identity control ($key)
    follow refs(before), ^docs { where ^path in list(after) }    forward over `before`, backward
                                                   over every doc whose `after` names me
  Per-occurrence metadata: $depth (seed = 1), $stop (interior|leaf|frontier|
  depth|cycle), $leaf/$frontier, $ordinal (a deterministic 1..N rank over the
  walk, ordered by depth then path — `order by $ordinal` for walk order,
  `where $ordinal <= N` for a deterministic budget cut), $key — usable in
  select/order by and the top-level post-walk where (a where conjunct that
  reads one filters the walk's RESULT; the other conjuncts remain the seed
  predicate), NOT metadata of the candidates a destination block's where reads,
  nor valid inside a consumer directive. Cyclic graphs are safe: a revisited
  node is admitted once as a `$stop == "cycle"` occurrence and never
  re-expanded. The default keeps one occurrence per distinct walk path;
  `follow distinct` dedups reached rows by identity.
  Destination blocks (OQX 0.20): a brace after ANY destination opens that
  destination's block — children { depth 2 }, refs(x) { depth 2 }, out_links
  collect { from dst depth 2 }, ^docs { where ^path in list(after) } — with the
  0.17 body rules (where-first, projections) and two clauses of its own after
  `where`: frontier <pred> (occurrences reached through this destination that
  match are frontiers; ^ there is the walk's enclosing scope) and depth <n>
  (this destination expands a frontier row only while $depth < n). The body
  that carries the follow may write frontier <pred> too, after its where and
  before follow: it applies to the SEEDS (read like the body's where) — a
  matching seed stays in the result with $stop == "frontier" and is not
  expanded; each destination's frontier is its own. There is no options block;
  the old `by` is $key. A bare follow ^docs (no brace, no consumer) is an
  error naming both block spellings.
  Type-preserving relations: block.children, section.children, section.subsections;
  the citation graph is out_links collect { from dst } / in_links collect { from doc }.
  from links where dst_path == "/notes/x.md"       inbound links to a doc, as rows
  select d: dst.title, k: dst_kind from links       the destination document's title
  from docs where out_links exists { where dst.layer == "draft" }   links into drafts
  select b: in_links collect distinct { from doc } from docs     backlinks as { id, path }
  select doc_id, dst_path from links where predicate == "depends_on"
  from docs where not doc.in_links exists { }      orphans (nothing links in)
  (The `graph` tool is a convenience wrapper that compiles to a follow query.)

## semantic grain

from docs ranks whole DOCUMENTS (one hit per file); from blocks ranks PASSAGES.
text()/where prune the candidate set; only order by reweights.

## Examples

  from docs where layer == "working"
  from docs where path.startsWith("/guides/") and updated_at >= "2026-08-01"
  select layer, tags from docs where "pricing" in list(tags)
  from docs where inline.owner == "alice"
  from docs where title.lower().contains("q3 plan")
  from docs where format == "yaml"
  from docs where type == "practitioner" order by era desc limit 2
  from docs where nodes none { where kind == "md:task" and not checked }
  from docs where tags exists { where $it == "tria-prima" }
  select fm: entries(data) collect { k: $key, v: $it } from docs where path == "/x.md"
  select owner_id, owner: ^nodes single { where kind == "person" and attrs.id == ^owner_id } from docs
  from blocks where type == "task" and not checked and under_heading("Launch") and doc.layer == "working"
  from blocks where type == "paragraph" and has_edge("references", "d_92aaaaa")
  select path, $depth from docs where path == "/timeline/review.md" follow refs(before), refs(after)
  select path, next: ^docs collect { path where ^path in list(before) } from docs where type == "milestone"
  select path, n: size(^docs), repo: ^id from docs limit 1
  select p: data.path, t: data.title from docs where has(data.path)
  docs { type == "substance" and not verified }
  select subject, process: ^docs[slug == ^subject]!.path from docs where type == "lab-note"
  select path, back: nodes first { select p: 0^docs collect { path where ^^path in list(after) } values } from docs where type == "milestone"
  select path, prior: refs(before) collect { path, when } from docs where type == "milestone"
  from blocks order by semantic("identity preservation across edits") desc limit 10
  select uri from links where dst_kind == "external"
  docs count { where layer == "canon" }
  select seq, origin, ts, hash from revisions where path == "/processes/calcination.md" order by seq desc
  from docs where revisions count { where origin == "api" } > 0
  select p: path, d: doc.path from revisions where doc == null
  select layer, n: count(), titles: collect(title), open: rows count { where nodes exists { where kind == "md:task" and not checked } } from docs group by layer having count() > 1 order by count() desc

Common mistake: `$path`/`$id` (the 2.x spelling) — omgbase has no $ names; write
`path`/`id`. Another: `where tags == "x"` on a list-valued key is false — write
`"x" in tags`. Another: `select data.path` — alias it (`p: data.path`).

hits.text: Calcination
Heating a substance in air until it is reduced to a friable powder — a *calx*. The first of the twelve gates and, in practice, the first thing anyone does.
element:: fire reversible:: no
Procedure
Grind the material, spread it thinly in an open crucible, and heat steadily below the melting point. Stir to expose fresh surface. Continue until no further weight is lost and no fumes come off.
crucible → grind → thin layer → moderate heat → stir → constant weight
The endpoint is the constant weight, not the colour. Colour tells you which oxide you have; weight tells you that you are finished.
What is actually happening

Organic matter burns away; metals take up oxygen. The characteristic *gain* in weight when calcining a metal is the observation that eventually broke the phlogiston theory — the calx weighs more than the metal, which a theory of escaping substance cannot accommodate.
Alchemical practice recorded this gain for centuries without drawing the inference. The data were sound; the framework could not use them.
Products
calcined lead → yellow massicot, then red minium calcined copper → black tenorite plant matter → ash, source of the [[salt]]
